Ente code_timer_progress.dart: full-width rounded bar (radius 2) height `isCompactMode ? 1 : 3` at top of card; `progress > 0.4 ? primary700 : Colors.orange`; ticks every 16 ms on mobile, 500 ms on desktop. Authenticator.cc EntryComponent.vue: `.sector` pie with `animationDuration: period + 's'` and `animationDelay: (sectorOffset % period) + 's'`; `timeout` class when `< 5` s remain; HOTP shows a redo icon instead. Note: none expose the timer to screen readers (Bitwarden marks it aria-hidden).

findings.claim: Every competitor shows a brand logo per entry, and the big three fetch it through their own proxy with a privacy toggle; the open-source apps bundle an icon pack. A monogram/generic icon is the fallback.
findings.detail: 1Password: "Rich icons are provided by 1Password" from `cache.agilebits.com`/`c.1password.com`; request carries IP, domain and user agent; toggle in extension Settings → "Appearance & shortcuts" → "Show app and website icons". Bitwarden: requests `https://icons.bitwarden.net/<hostname>/icon.png`, cached on Fastly; "a request for an icon contains the hostname of the website stored in your vault"; when disabled shows "a generic, locally accessed icon". Proton Pass Display settings: "Show website favicons — Proton Pass will display the item favicon via Proton anonymized image proxy." Ente Auth: "uses the icon pack from simple-icons" plus a `custom-icons.json` (fields `title`, optional `slug`, `hex`, `altNames`; SVG ≤20 KB; matched on issuer text before the first "." or "(" with spaces removed); icon widths 24 px small, 32 px compact-large, 42 px large; v4.4.23 fixed "custom icons for visibility, contrast, colour, and flickering in light and dark mode"; v4.4.15 added an icon picker. 2FAS: icons arrive only via company submission ("When your brand icon is accepted, it will be uploaded up to 3 weeks"); App Store reviewer: "New icon submissions take months to add". Implementable: bundle a slug-matched SVG set, let users pick an icon, fall back to a two-letter monogram, and offer a "load favicons" toggle.

findings.claim: Chrome gives extensions a first-party favicon endpoint, so an MV3 authenticator can show a site logo for any saved domain without a third-party proxy.
findings.detail: URL pattern `chrome-extension://EXTENSION_ID/_favicon/?pageUrl=EXAMPLE_URL&size=FAV_SIZE`, built with `runtime.getURL("/_favicon/")`. Requires the `"favicon"` permission; "The 'favicon' permission triggers a warning unless paired with an existing permission (such as 'tabs') that supersedes it." Favicons "are treated as resources under your extension's origin"; to use them in content scripts declare `_favicon/*` in `web_accessible_resources` with `matches: ["<all_urls>"]`, `extension_ids: ["*"]`. "The most common size is 16 x 16 pixels"; the sample uses 32. Only works for sites in the user's history/favicon cache, so pair it with a bundled pack + monogram fallback.

findings.claim: Free brand-logo sets and their licences: Simple Icons (CC0-1.0, 3,400+), Dashboard Icons (Apache-2.0, 3,400+, light/dark variants), selfh.st icons (CC-BY-4.0, standard/dark/light), aegis-icons (CC0-1.0, monochrome). All disclaim trademarks; CC0 covers the SVG, not the brand.
findings.detail: Simple Icons: "CC0-1.0 license"; CDN `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/simple-icons@v16/icons/[ICON SLUG].svg` or `https://unpkg.com/simple-icons@v16/icons/[ICON SLUG].svg`; colour CDN `https://cdn.simpleicons.org/[ICON SLUG]/[COLOR]/[DARK_MODE_COLOR]` (dark colour follows prefers-color-scheme); npm `simple-icons` exposes `hex` per icon. Disclaimer: "Simple Icons is released under CC0 - though that doesn't mean to imply that all icons within the project are also CC0"; users should "read these guidelines and ensure their usage of the brand's icon is in accordance with them"; brands can request removal. Dashboard Icons (homarr-labs): "Apache-2.0 license", "over 3,400" icons, SVG + auto-generated 512 px PNG/WEBP, CDN `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/homarr-labs/dashboard-icons/svg/<name>.svg`, `-light` suffix for dark backgrounds, `-dark` for light; "Icons are used for identification purposes only and do not imply endorsement." selfh.st icons: "CC-BY-4.0 license" (attribution required); SVG (most), PNG/WebP/AVIF (all), ICO 16–128 px; "provides SVG icons (when available) in standard, dark, and light colors"; served via jsDelivr `gh/selfhst/icons`. aegis-icons: "monochrome-styled 2FA icons", CC0-1.0 but "applies only to templates, texts, codes and some of the icons"; ships `pack.json` manifest; takedown contact. 2FAS has no public icon repo; its extension README says "the graphics used in this app are not part of the open source project". Ente uses Simple Icons in production, which is the precedent for an authenticator.

findings.claim: Tap/click-to-copy with an immediate toast is universal, and users explicitly ask for it back when it is removed; several apps also auto-copy the TOTP after autofill.
findings.detail: Ente: tap copies and shows `copiedToClipboard`; tapping the grey next code copies it with `copiedNextToClipboard`; Android can minimise the app on copy. 2FAS: "Quick Copy: Tap on a token to copy it instantly." Authenticator.cc: click or Enter → `copyCode`, writes clipboard, shows `i18n.copied`; if autofill is enabled it first injects the content script and sends a `pastecode` message to the tab. Bitwarden: copy button `[appCopyClick]` with `showToast`; keyboard-shortcut page: after autofill "the code is copied to the clipboard automatically" when the login has a TOTP; blog re-added "Show quick copy actions on Vault" (one-click copy of username/password/TOTP per row) after redesign feedback. Proton ValueControl: `clickToCopy` wraps the value, `cursor-pointer`, hidden placeholder `'••••••••••••'`. App Store review of Ente: "see the upcoming codes in addition to the current codes" praised; 2FAS reviewer requested codes "collapse to hide until clicked on".

findings.claim: Keyboard-first behaviour is documented as a feature by 1Password and Bitwarden: a global open shortcut, type-to-search on open, Esc to clear/close, arrow-key navigation, Enter to fill, and dedicated copy-OTP shortcuts.
findings.detail: 1Password in the browser: open/close pop-up Ctrl+Shift+X (Chrome/Edge/Brave), Ctrl+. (Firefox); "open the pop-up and start typing" to search; Esc clears search / closes; arrow keys move between items; Ctrl+Enter autofill; Ctrl+C copy username; Ctrl+Shift+C copy password; Ctrl+Shift+Win+C copy one-time password; Ctrl+I new item; Ctrl+E edit; hold Ctrl+Alt to reveal secure fields. Bitwarden: Ctrl+Shift+Y open, Ctrl+Shift+L autofill (press again to cycle matches), Ctrl+Shift+9 generate password, Ctrl+Shift+N lock; search field activates when the extension opens. Ente: "Focus search on app start" option and "Type-to-search on desktop" (v4.4.26), tag chips keyboard-accessible (v4.4.23). 2FAS: "Active Search" opens keyboard immediately. Raycast's redesign puts actions and their shortcuts in a bottom action bar "which helps users learn shortcuts". Chrome commands API: "may specify at most four suggested keyboard shortcuts"; "must include either Ctrl or Alt"; Ctrl+Alt combos forbidden; `_execute_action` opens the popup; users rebind at chrome://extensions/shortcuts; global commands limited to Ctrl+Shift+[0..9].

findings.claim: Pinning/favourites, drag-to-reorder, tags/groups and hide-codes are the standard organisation set; pinned entries get a visible marker and sit at the top.
findings.detail: Ente: pin via long-press/right-click → "Pin"; pinned card draws a 39x39 px (24 px compact) triangle `PinBgPainter` top-right with a pin SVG and `pinnedCardBoxShadow`; pins ignored when sort is manual; tags filter the list; custom sort / reorder page; multi-select bulk actions; "Hide codes" with double-tap reveal. 2FAS: unlimited groups, default "My Tokens" group; "Set List Order: Choose between alphabetical (A-Z) or manual order" with drag, "Manual sorting is saved even when switching back from/to A-Z"; hide-all-tokens option. Authenticator.cc: pin icon commits `pinEntry` and scrolls list to top; `movehandle` drag bars per entry; "Smart filter" auto-filters entries to the current site. Bitwarden: "Favorites appear in a section above All items", collapsible via `bit-disclosure`, starred from Edit view. 1Password: favourite via ellipsis menu; "Filter list" per vault; "All Accounts" view.

findings.claim: Large vaults are handled with virtualised lists plus collapsible sections and hover-revealed row actions (Bitwarden, Proton), not pagination.
findings.detail: Bitwarden vault-list-items-container: `<cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport [itemSize]="itemHeight$ | async" bitScrollLayout>` with `*cdkVirtualFor`; each group is a `<bit-section>` whose header toggles a `<bit-disclosure>` (chevron `bwi-angle-up/down`); per row: `<app-vault-icon>` start slot, a "Fill" text button shown on hover/focus (`showFillTextOnHover`), launch (`bwi-external-link`), `<app-item-copy-actions>`, `<app-item-more-options>`, paperclip for attachments. Proton Pass VirtualList.tsx: `import { AutoSizer, List } from 'react-virtualized'`, caller-supplied `rowHeight(index)`, top/bottom scroll shadows as scroll affordance, `onScrollEnd` when reaching bottom. Chrome's side panel (Chrome 114+) "remains open when navigating between tabs" and can be toggled from the action icon with `openPanelOnActionClick` — an option for users with many accounts who want a persistent list.

findings.claim: Dark mode is offered as Light / Dark / System everywhere, implemented with semantic colour tokens on a theme class; Bitwarden's token values are public.
findings.detail: Bitwarden tw-theme.css: light `--color-text-main: 27 32 41`, `--color-bg-primary: var(--color-white)`, `--color-primary-600: 23 93 220`, `--color-danger-600: 203 38 58`; `.theme_dark` overrides `--color-bg-primary: var(--color-gray-900)`, `--color-text-main: 243 246 249`, `--color-primary-600: 101 171 255`, `--color-danger-600: 255 78 99`; Tailwind config uses `rgb(var(--color-x) / <alpha-value>)`, prefix `tw-`, preflight off; token families `text-main/muted/contrast/code`, `bg-*`, `fg-*`, `border-*`, `hover-*`. Help page: "Switch between light mode, dark mode, or align Bitwarden with your system default." Proton Pass PassThemeCardList: "Automatic" (`PassThemeOption.OS`, "Proton Pass will follow your system theme."), "Dark", "Light"; OTPDonut re-reads its CSS-variable colours on a dark-theme media listener. Ente changelog v4.4.23: "Desktop theme persists after unlocking"; Linux title bar follows GNOME dark setting (v4.4.24). Authenticator.cc themes: "normal", "dark", "simple", "compact", "accessibility", "flat".

findings.claim: Motion is short (≈180 ms), limited to fades/scale on state change and view slides, user-switchable, and should respect prefers-reduced-motion.
findings.detail: Ente code tile: `AnimatedContainer` 180 ms for background/selection colour, `AnimatedOpacity` 180 ms for selection border, `AnimatedSwitcher` 180 ms (fade, plus scale for the check indicator) for the timer and selection check. Proton donut wrapper uses `anime-fade-in` on mount. Bitwarden exposes "Show animations ... for example a slide effect when you change views" and ships `vault-fade-in-out` and `vault-loading-skeleton` components for list loading. MDN: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` "Indicates that a user has enabled the setting on their device for reduced motion"; replace scale/slide with opacity changes under it.

findings.claim: Onboarding/empty-state conventions: Bitwarden ships an intro carousel and a filters tour inside the popup; Ente iterated its new-user flow; Google says onboarding starts in the store listing; NN/g says an empty state must state status, explain what goes there and link straight to the creating action.
findings.detail: Bitwarden popup component folders include `intro-carousel`, `vault-filters-tour`, `at-risk-callout`, `vault-loading-skeleton` (names only; contents not read). Ente changelog: "Improved new-user experience" (v4.4.12), "New login and sign-up screens" (v4.4.17), "Design refresh across settings, setup, imports, and code management" (v4.4.25). Chrome Web Store best practices: onboarding begins by "providing screenshots and a video of how the extension works"; the listing "should explicitly communicate what the extension does"; images should not be "blurry or too busy"; give users "a simple, intuitive, and seamless user interface". `runtime.onInstalled` fires with `reason: "install"` (also update/chrome_update/shared_module_update) — the hook for opening a one-time welcome page. NN/g: "Do not default to totally empty states"; show a status message, say "what could be displayed, and how to populate the area with that content", and give "direct pathways (i.e., links) to getting started with key tasks" (e.g. DataDog's "Star your favorites to list them here").

findings.claim: Ente's "Share code" is the only shipped reference for the user's requested share-a-code link feature: a time-boxed view (2/5/10 min) that reveals rolling codes without the secret, TOTP-only.
findings.detail: Ente features page: long-press/right-click a code → "Share" → pick a 2-, 5-, or 10-minute window; "Recipients see codes for that window without access to the secret key." Changelog v4.4.23: "Share option limited to TOTP codes and hidden for HOTP." 2FAS v5.3.15 added "QR code generation for sharing" (sharing the secret, not a timed link). 2FAS also runs a separate open-source `2fas-share` service ("Shares short text securely via a single link", GPL-3.0). Ente's `share` UI folder exists at mobile/apps/auth/lib/ui/share.

findings.claim: Public design-system material: 1Password's "Knox" design language (1Password 8) and its 2023 brand refresh; Bitwarden's open Angular/Tailwind component library and Dec 2024 redesign post; Proton's unified design system and "new visual universe"; Raycast's "A fresh look and feel". None publish an extension-specific UI spec.
findings.detail: 1Password 8 blog: "We created an entirely new design language, code-named Knox"; "The new design language extends seamlessly into 1Password for Safari"; no values given. 1Password brand refresh (Apr 2023): bespoke typeface "Agile Sans" for the wordmark; core colours "Bits Blue, Intrepid Blue, and ... Biscuit"; Core Blue "desaturated a bit so it feels more tactile and almost denim-like"; "the 1Password icon in your browser is staying the same". Bitwarden: `libs/components` is "Bitwarden's shared Angular component library" (Tailwind `prefix: "tw-"`, `corePlugins.preflight: false`, font sizes with 150% line-height); redesign post lists New dropdown, Fill button, merged Tab+Vault view, filters in main view, compact mode (beta), light/dark, width options. Proton "new visual universe": brand typeface ABC Arizona (Sans body, Flare headlines) by Dinamo; a bolder purple "compatible with light and dark backgrounds"; each product icon "starts with the Proton purple and then fades into the service color"; design-system.protontech.ch exists but is a Storybook SPA (could not be read). Raycast: principles "fast, simple, and delightful"; "We've made the bar bigger to reflect its importance"; larger leading icons in results; outline icons with heavier strokes and consistent stroke width/corner radius (James McDonald); bottom action bar listing actions with shortcuts; Compact Mode. Third-party "Raycast design system" pages (Inter, near-black, red accent) are unofficial.

findings.claim: Review sentiment that maps to design: Ente is praised as "gorgeous"/"polished" with next-code preview; 2FAS for a "great user interface" but slow icon additions; Bitwarden post-redesign reviews focus on popup slowness and width; Authenticator.cc on backup reminders. Chrome Web Store review pages could not be read (consent wall).
findings.detail: Ente App Store (4.7, 290 ratings): "Absolutely gorgeous interface, simple to use, clean"; "works flawlessly while looking good doing it"; "see the upcoming codes in addition to the current codes"; Product Hunt: "super polished". 2FAS App Store: "it has a great user interface"; request for "bubble tiles" and codes that "collapse to hide until clicked on"; "New icon submissions take months to add". Bitwarden AMO (page 1 of 375): "it often takes several seconds to show the pop-out"; "isn't quite as polished as 1Password" (still 5★). Authenticator.cc AMO: "Super easy to use and reminds me to make backups"; "Backup nags and minor annoyances, otherwise perfect". Chrome Web Store listing/review URLs redirect to consent.google.com, so store-review text for Authenticator and Proton Pass was not retrievable.

findings.claim: Unconfirmed items (low confidence): Bitwarden's current `--font-sans` value, 2FAS's icon file spec, and the Chromium constant names behind the 800x600 clamp.
findings.detail: Bitwarden's new Tailwind theme references `var(--font-sans)` but the variable is not defined in tw-theme.css (33 KB, fully read) and base.scss returned 404; only the legacy popup SCSS names Inter. A search snippet says 2FAS's branding ToS defines an icon as a PNG of at least 120x120 px, but the ToS page itself was not fetched. Chromium's extension_popup.h defines `kMinSize = extensions::kExtensionPopupMinSize` and `kMaxSize = extensions::kExtensionPopupMaxSize` (comment: "The maximum is an arbitrary number and should be smaller than most screens") without the literal values; the 25x25/800x600 figures are confirmed only by Google's action API doc and third-party guides.

research.summary: Researched how authenticator and password-manager products share TOTP seeds and one-time codes, what security guidance and Chrome Web Store policy require, and what zero-server designs exist. Two clear patterns emerged. (1) Seed transfer: otpauth:// QR scanned locally (Ente "QR", Key URI format), Google Authenticator's otpauth-migration protobuf QR for bulk moves, or shared vaults (1Password, Bitwarden orgs, Proton Pass items, Apple Shared Groups) with membership-based revocation. (2) Code-only sharing: Ente Auth is the only authenticator found that shares codes without the secret, and its design is directly reusable by a Chrome extension with a GitHub Pages site: pre-compute ceil(duration*60/period) codes for 2/5/10 min, encrypt with a random 256-bit key, put ciphertext in the query string and the key only in the URL fragment, and have a static page decrypt in the browser with a live countdown and "expired"/"clock out of sync" states. Key in fragment is the industry norm (Bitwarden Send, Proton Pass, Keeper, Excalidraw, PrivateBin) because fragments are never sent to the server (MDN, RFC 3986). Server-backed products add view-count limits, device-locking and revocation; a serverless link can only enforce time expiry. Google's own help tells users "Never share your verification codes with anyone", so a share UI needs an explicit warning. Chrome Web Store policy counts authentication information as sensitive user data, treats transmission as "handling", requires modern cryptography in transit, a privacy policy, in-product prominent disclosure/consent, and disclosure of data-practice changes after install. navigator.share in an extension popup is unconfirmed; desktop Chrome supports it fully only since 128 and Ente itself hides "Send" on Windows/Linux, so copy-link + local QR is the safe fallback. Unconfirmed items are marked low confidence.

findings.claim: Google Authenticator transfers accounts between devices with QR codes that embed the raw secrets in an undocumented otpauth-migration protobuf; there is no expiry or revocation.
findings.detail: Google's help page: on the old device open Menu > Transfer codes > Export codes, unlock, select accounts; 'If you transfer more than one account, your old device may create more than one QR code.' On the new device: Menu > Transfer codes > Import codes and scan. The QR payload is `otpauth-migration://offline?data=<base64>` where data is a protobuf `Payload { repeated OtpParameters otp_parameters; int32 version; int32 batch_size; int32 batch_index; int32 batch_id }` and `OtpParameters { bytes secret; string name; string issuer; Algorithm algorithm (SHA1/SHA256/SHA512/MD5); DigitCount digits (SIX/EIGHT); OtpType type (HOTP/TOTP); uint64 counter; string unique_id }` (schema from the reverse-engineered dim13/otpauth project; Google does not document it). Design to borrow: if AuthPeek wants a 'Move to Google Authenticator' QR, emit this protobuf; for every other app emit standard otpauth:// QRs. Cloud sync via Google Account: 'Google encrypts Authenticator codes both in transit and at rest' (not stated as end-to-end).

findings.claim: Google Authenticator's cloud sync was criticised in 2023 for not being end-to-end encrypted; Google promised E2EE, but no primary source confirms it has shipped as of 2026-10.
findings.detail: BleepingComputer/TechRadar coverage (2023) reports Mysk's finding that synced secrets were not E2EE and Google's statement that E2EE would come 'in the future'. The only 2026 source found is a non-primary guide saying it 'isn't universally live'. Treat Google Authenticator sync as 'encrypted by Google, not zero-knowledge' unless Google's help page changes.

findings.claim: Ente Auth is the only authenticator found that shares only codes (not the secret): a 2/5/10-minute link with pre-computed codes, encrypted with a key kept in the URL fragment, decrypted by a static web page.
findings.detail: Help page: long-press/right-click a code > Share > choose 2, 5 or 10 minutes; 'After the link expires, the recipients will no longer be able to view new codes.' Blog: 'Ente will pre-compute the codes for this duration, and share those within the link, end-to-end encrypted' and 'Your 2FA secret / seed phrase is not shared'. Source (mobile/apps/auth/lib/ui/share/code_share.dart): `count = ((durationInMin * 60.0) / code.period).ceil()`; payload JSON `{startTime, step, codes: 'c1,c2,...'}`; `_generate256BitKey()` with `Random.secure()`; `CryptoUtil.encryptData(input, key)` returns encryptedData + header (libsodium-style; exact cipher not fetched); URL = `https://auth.ente.com/share?data=<b64url ct>&header=<b64url hdr>#<b64url key>`; shared via the OS share sheet (share_plus). Web page (web/apps/auth/src/pages/share.tsx) reads `data`/`header` from the query string and the key from `window.location.hash.substring(1)`, decrypts in-browser, computes `index = floor((now-startTime)/step)`, shows the current code large, the next code small ('next' / 'Last code'), a progress bar that turns warning-coloured when <40% remains, and messages 'Decrypting...', 'The code has expired.', and 'Your or the person who shared the code has out of sync time.' The link is self-contained: no server state, so nothing to revoke; only time expiry. Also: `showShareDialog` checks `code.type.canShareCodes` (not all types shareable). This is the design AuthPeek can copy almost 1:1 using its GitHub Pages site as the viewer.

findings.claim: Ente Auth also offers a 'QR' action that exposes the full entry including the secret for scanning into another app, and exports in plain text or as an encrypted file.
findings.detail: Help page: long-press/right-click > 'QR' — 'This allows you to easily share the complete entry (including the secret) with others by letting them scan the displayed QR code.' Export: 'Export your codes in plain text, as an encrypted file, or automatically via the CLI.' Two-tier model to borrow: 'Share codes' (no secret, expiring) vs 'Show QR / Move account' (secret, explicit).

findings.claim: Authy multi-device shares the user's own tokens across devices via encryption with a backup password that never reaches Twilio; a new device is approved from an existing device and can be removed from Settings > Devices.
findings.detail: Twilio blog: on the new device enter the phone number, choose 'Use Existing Device', approve on the primary device; 'all of your authentication tokens are encrypted locally: no tokens are kept on Authy's servers'; before disposing of a device 'remove access by that device in your Authy account settings'; turn off 'Allow Multi-device' after enrolling to block new devices. Twilio support article (search snippet; direct fetch returned 403): the backup password 'is used to create a secure key for encrypting all of your configured Authy 2FA account tokens' and 'is never sent or stored in our servers'; without it on any device tokens are 'permanently inaccessible'. No Authy 'share a code with someone else' feature was found.

findings.claim: 2FAS moves tokens between phones only via same-OS cloud backup or a password-protected export file (no phone-to-phone QR); its browser extension is paired by the extension showing a QR that the phone scans, after which codes are delivered to the browser on request, end-to-end encrypted, and the extension never holds secrets.
findings.detail: 2FAS sync page: 'Cloud synchronization (iOS – iCloud, Android – Google Drive)' for same-OS; cross-platform: 'export a backup file with all the tokens/codes to an external device such as a USB stick or Mac/PC' and 'remember to set up a password for it'. Pairing page: Settings > Browser Extension > 'Pair with a web browser' on the phone, scan the QR shown in the extension's options; the phone asks to trust the browser; login requests arrive as push notifications and the token is passed over an end-to-end encrypted connection (vendor claim; protocol not documented). Relevant precedent for an 'extension renders QR, phone scans it' handoff.

findings.claim: 1Password shares TOTP secrets by moving the Login item into a shared vault, or sends a snapshot copy via an expiring link (1h/1d/7d/14d/30d, optional one-time view, anyone-with-link or verified emails, deletable from Sharing History).
findings.detail: One-time passwords page: 'You can share logins with one-time passwords by moving them to vaults you've shared with your family or team' and 'You can also share these logins with people outside of 1Password'. Share-items page: 'Choose when the link expires and who to share it with'; recipients 'don't need a 1Password account'; email-restricted links require an emailed verification code; revoke via View Sharing History > Delete Link; 'Your changes won't be shared until you share the item again' (snapshot). SDK docs: `expireAfter` ∈ {OneHour, OneDay, SevenDays, FourteenDays, ThirtyDays}; boolean `oneTimeOnly`; individual/family defaults: unlimited views, max 30 days, default 7 days; Business validates against the admin's item-sharing policy. 1Password blog: viewer sees 'the web view of the shared item exactly as it exists in 1Password' including extra fields. Not confirmed anywhere whether the link viewer renders a live TOTP code (low confidence on that sub-point).

findings.claim: Bitwarden stores TOTP as an 'Authenticator key' (otpauth:// or steam:// URI) in the login item; generating codes needs Premium or a paid organisation, which is also how the secret is shared with a team.
findings.detail: 'Paste the secret key into the Authenticator Key field'; parameters 'can be customized in Bitwarden by manually editing the otpauth://totp/ URI'; Steam secrets entered as `steam://your_secret_key_here` (5-char codes); 'Storing keys in Password Manager integrated authenticator is available to all accounts. Generating TOTP codes is available with Premium or membership to a paid organization (Families, Teams, or Enterprise).' The page does not explicitly state that collection members all see codes (inferred from org membership requirement).

findings.claim: Bitwarden Send is the reference design for an expiring, view-limited, revocable text share with the key in the URL fragment: 1,000-char text, 7-day default/31-day max deletion, optional expiry, max access count, optional password, manual delete.
findings.detail: Lifespan: 'By default, Sends will automatically be deleted seven days after they are created', 'maximum allowed value of 31 days from creation'; expiration date (web/desktop only) presets 1 hour/1 day/7 days or custom; max access count: when reached recipients see the Send 'doesn't exist or is no longer available', sender sees 'Max access count reached'; text Sends count link visits; you can 'manually deactivate or delete a Send at any time'. Create: 'Text Sends can include up to 1,000 characters encrypted' (encryption adds 30–50%); 'Hide text by default'; 'Hide your email address from viewers'; text Sends free, file Sends premium. Encryption: a new 128-bit secret per Send, HKDF-SHA256 -> 512-bit key, AES-256 for data and metadata; link format `https://vault.bitwarden.com/#/send_id/encryption_key`; 'The anchor/fragment/hash is not sent to the server'; 'The encryption key is never included in network requests'; password is only an access check and 'is not involved in the encryption'; tip: send the link without the key and share the key through a separate channel.

findings.claim: Proton Pass secure links put a locally generated link key after '#', support expiry plus a view-count limit with usage monitoring, and can be revoked with 'Remove link'; sharing items with other Pass users (read-only or write) requires a paid plan.
findings.detail: URL form `https://pass.proton.me/s/RANDOM_TOKEN#link_key`; device generates 'A random link key (share secret)', encrypts the item key with it, and encrypts the link key with the vault key so the owner can recover the link; 'At no point does Proton have access to the link key'; set expiry and 'decide how many times the link can be used'; 'monitor how many times the link has been used'; delete so 'it can never be used again'. Warnings: use a secure channel; anyone with the 'full share URL' can access within expiry/use limit; update the password or enable 2FA after sharing. Item sharing with users: 'Recipients can receive write or read-only permissions' under 'Shared with me'; single-item sharing needs Pass Plus/Professional (BetaNews reports 1 hour–30 day expiry range; third-party).

findings.claim: Apple Passwords Shared Groups share passwords, passkeys and Sign in with Apple credentials with trusted contacts via iCloud Keychain; only the creator manages membership; Apple's docs never list verification codes as shareable.
findings.detail: Apple: a Shared Group is 'an easy, secure way to share passwords, passkeys, and Sign in with Apple credentials' with 'your family and other trusted contacts'; Mac guide: 'Select passwords, passkeys, and Sign in with Apple accounts to move to the group', 'A password, passkey, or Sign in with Apple account can only be shared with one group', 'All people in the group can change the account passwords and passkeys you share', 'only you can add and remove people from the group'. Verification codes are set up by pasting a setup key ('Set Up Code'); the verification-codes guide does not mention groups. Whether a code attached to a shared password travels with it is not stated in any Apple page found (low confidence on that point). Requirements: iOS 17/iPadOS 17/macOS 14+.

findings.claim: Keeper One-Time Share adds device-locking on top of fragment-key links: the token after '#' never reaches Keeper, the first device to open the link binds it, and the server deletes the encrypted record key so the token cannot be reused; expiry up to 180 days; instant revocation.
findings.detail: Expiry options '1 hour, 24 hours, 1 week, 30 days, 90 days, or a custom date and time (up to 180 days)'; the share 'can only be used on one device'; recipients need no account; trash icon 'will immediately disable the share link'. Encryption model: 256-bit AES record key encrypted with the one-time token; token sent 'by URL or QR code', 'held within the "fragment identifier" section of the URL' and 'never sent over the network to Keeper's servers'; recipient device generates an EC key pair, authenticates with a hash of the token, decrypts the record key locally, server deletes the encrypted record key for that device, later requests are ECDSA-signed. Shows what a server enables (device-lock, view-once, revoke) that a serverless design cannot.

findings.claim: Team 'share the current code' in chat is done either by a bot that holds the TOTP secret (open-source Keystone: /keystone slash command) or, per GitHub's guidance, by storing the TOTP secret in the org password manager and restricting access; no vendor Slack integration posts codes.
findings.detail: Keystone (DFurnes/keystone, Slack Bolt): 'Just type /keystone in the configured channel to be granted a new two-factor code'; secret in `TOTP_SECRET` env var as 'otpauth://totp/...'; 'Optionally, set KEYSTONE_CHANNEL to limit Keystone usage to a specific channel'; no per-user access control. GitHub docs for shared bot/service accounts: store the TOTP secret 'in the password manager your organization uses', restrict to a controlled mailing list, generate codes with a CLI such as oathtool. Authn8 is a commercial 'team authenticator' that markets against 'screenshotting QR codes or texting OTPs over Slack' (vendor claim).

findings.claim: NIST SP 800-63B-4 permits exporting OTP secret keys at AAL1/AAL2 (to a 'sync fabric' meeting Appendix B.2) and prohibits it at AAL3; it requires secrets to be 'strongly protected against unauthorized disclosure' and places responsibility on subscribers not to disclose them, but has no normative rule against a subscriber sharing a code.
findings.detail: §3.1.4.1: 'the subscriber MAY export the secret key and store it in a sync fabric that meets the requirements in Appendix B.2'; §3.1.4.2 / §3.1.5.2: symmetric keys 'SHALL be strongly protected against unauthorized disclosure'; §2.3.2: 'syncable authenticators SHALL NOT be used at AAL3'; Table 1 Key Exportability: permitted AAL1/AAL2, prohibited AAL3; §3.2.5: manual-entry OTP 'SHALL NOT be considered phishing-resistant'; Introduction (informative): 'subscribers are responsible for protecting their authentication secrets and not disclosing them to others'. Implication: a share feature is within NIST's model if the exported secret stays encrypted end to end.

findings.claim: Google's own user guidance is categorical: 'Never share your verification codes with anyone, as scammers may try to take over your account.' A share feature should therefore carry an explicit, non-dismissable warning and must never look like a prompt asking for a code.
findings.detail: 2-Step Verification help: 'Never share your verification codes with anyone, as scammers may try to take over your account.', 'You won't receive a call from Google to verify a code.', 'Do not give out your backup codes to anyone.' Google Voice help, heading 'Don't share your verification code with anyone': 'it's important you don't reply to any requests for your verification code', 'Google employees will never ask for this code.' Proton and Bitwarden both tell senders to use a secure/separate channel for the link or key.

findings.claim: Academic and industry sources treat QR screenshots and plaintext secret exports as credential leaks: a USENIX Security 2023 study of 22 Android TOTP apps found backup mechanisms with 'serious cryptographic flaws' and some that let developers read secrets in plaintext.
findings.detail: Gilsenan et al. (USENIX Sec '23): 22 Play Store TOTP apps (≥100k installs) with backup; 'most backup strategies end up placing trust in the same technologies that TOTP 2FA is meant to supersede' (passwords, SMS, email); some 'allowed the app developers to access the TOTP secrets in plaintext'. Atos security research: attackers hunting 2FA material look for QR codes saved as images and screenshots; leaked provisioning codes turn MFA into single-factor. The Authenticator.cc extension docs: 'It is strongly recommended to only use password-protected backups.' Design consequence: never produce a persisted artifact (image file, plaintext otpauth link) by default; render QR on screen only, and encrypt any exported file.

findings.claim: Chrome Web Store policy treats authentication information as personal/sensitive user data and counts transmitting it as 'handling': a share feature that sends anything off-device requires modern cryptography in transit, a privacy policy, in-product prominent disclosure and consent, Limited Use compliance, and disclosure of the changed data practice after install.
findings.detail: User Data FAQ: 'by "handle" we mean collecting, transmitting, using, or sharing user data'; examples include 'Authentication information (such as logins, password, and authentication cookies)'; 'This policy requires all Products that handle user information to post a privacy policy' (even when data stays on device, FAQ 3); 'Handle the user data securely, including transmitting it via modern cryptography'; 'Extensions must transmit user data over a secure connection (e.g. HTTPS, WSS)'; 'The prominent disclosure and consent must occur within the Product's user interface' and 'must not be located only in a privacy policy'; exemption for transmissions to a native program on the same computer. Handling Requirements: 'Keep authentication information secure. Don't publicly disclose authentication information.' Disclosure Requirements: before install 'Prominently disclose what user data will be collected and how it will be used' and 'Obtain the user's affirmative and informed consent'; 'If an extension introduces different user data practices after installation, the extension must prominently disclose data practice changes.' Limited Use: 'Extensions may only collect, use, or transmit user data that is necessary for the extension's disclosed single purpose'; 'All other transfers of personal or sensitive user data are completely prohibited'; an affirmative Limited Use statement must appear on a website belonging to the extension. Privacy Policy: 'If your Product handles any user data, then you must post an accurate and up to date privacy policy' disclosing 'All parties the user data will be shared with'. Dashboard: disclose data types collected and certify Limited Use compliance in the Privacy practices tab. Practical reading: a fragment-only payload (never transmitted) is the lightest-touch design; an Ente-style ciphertext-in-query-string to a GitHub Pages page is a transmission of encrypted user data to GitHub's servers and should be disclosed.

findings.claim: Putting the secret or key in the URL fragment keeps it off every server: MDN and RFC 3986 confirm the fragment is processed only by the client, and Bitwarden Send, Proton Pass, Keeper, Ente Auth, Excalidraw and PrivateBin all rely on this.
findings.detail: MDN: 'The fragment is not sent to the server when the URI is requested; it is processed by the client (e.g., the browser) after the resource is retrieved.' RFC 3986 §3.5: 'the fragment identifier is separated from the rest of the URI prior to a dereference' and 'the identifying information within the fragment itself is dereferenced solely by the user agent'. Excalidraw links are `excalidraw.com/#json=<id>,<key>` with a client-generated AES key after '#', server stores only an encrypted blob. PrivateBin: random AES-256 key generated in-browser, key in fragment, only ciphertext uploaded (server still logs IP/time per URL). Residual risk named by Proton: anyone holding the full URL can open it within limits; Bitwarden's mitigation is sending the key through a second channel. A fully serverless variant for AuthPeek: `https://lazizjanasatov.github.io/Authpeek/share#<ciphertext+key or payload>` so GitHub never receives even the ciphertext; the same fragment can be pasted into the extension popup on another computer and parsed with `location.hash`/`new URL(...).hash`.

findings.claim: A locally rendered otpauth:// QR is the universal way to hand a TOTP account to a phone: the Key URI format is `otpauth://TYPE/LABEL?secret=BASE32&issuer=...` with optional algorithm/digits/period, and Signal/2FAS show the 'computer renders QR, phone scans' handoff pattern.
findings.detail: Key URI format (Google wiki, archived): `otpauth://TYPE/LABEL?PARAMETERS`; TYPE totp|hotp; LABEL `issuer:accountname` (URL-encoded, no colons inside parts); `secret` Base32 (RFC 3548) with padding omitted; `issuer` strongly recommended and should match the label prefix; `algorithm` SHA1 (default)/SHA256/SHA512, `digits` 6|8, `period` default 30, `counter` for hotp — algorithm/digits/period 'ignored by the Google Authenticator implementations'. Authenticator.cc import docs recommend scanning about 'five accounts at one time' to avoid QR read errors. Signal device linking (server docs via mirror): the new device opens a provisioning socket, gets a temporary 'provisioning address', displays that address plus a public key as a QR; the primary device scans it and sends 'an encrypted provisioning message' relayed once by the server — a model for a phone-to-extension push where the QR carries only a public key, never the secret. 2FAS pairing uses the same extension-shows-QR direction.

findings.claim: navigator.share requires a secure context, transient user activation and the web-share permission; chrome-extension:// counts as a secure origin in Chromium, but desktop support is recent and uneven (Chrome full only since 128; 89–127 ChromeOS/Windows only; Edge 93+; Firefox desktop behind a flag), and no source confirms it works inside an extension popup.
findings.detail: MDN: 'This method requires that the current document have the web-share Permissions Policy and transient activation'; errors: NotAllowedError (policy blocked / no transient activation), InvalidStateError (another share in progress), AbortError (cancelled or 'no share targets available'), DataError. Chromium secure-origins list includes '(chrome-extension, *, —)'. MDN compat data: Chrome desktop partial 89–128 with note 'Only supported on ChromeOS and Windows', full from 128; Edge partial 81–93 'Only supported on Windows', full 93+; Firefox 71+ behind `dom.webshare.enabled`; Safari 12.1+. caniuse: Firefox desktop unsupported through 161. Ente's own desktop share helper hides the 'Send' button on Windows/Linux and offers only 'Save' (share_utils.dart: `if (!Platform.isWindows && !Platform.isLinux)`), so even a native app distrusts desktop share sheets. Safe design: feature-detect `navigator.share` inside the click handler, fall back to Copy link + on-screen QR.

findings.claim: The most-installed competing extension (Authenticator by mymindstorm, authenticator.cc) handles cross-device moves with password-protected or 'standard format' backups, cloud backup to Drive/OneDrive/Dropbox, and import from backup file, QR screenshots or otpauth text; it has no person-to-person share feature.
findings.detail: Docs: 'Download Password-Protected Backup' appears only after a password is set in Settings > Security; unencrypted 'Download Backup File' uses 'a standardized backup format that can be imported to other OTP clients' (interoperable with FreeOTP+, Aegis plain-text import, GNOME Authenticator; encrypted backups not supported by those); cloud backups saved to an 'Authenticator Backups' folder as yyyymmdd.json; imports: 'Import Backup File' (.json/.txt, password prompt if encrypted), 'Import QR Image Backup' (multiple images; ~5 accounts at a time recommended), 'Import Text Backup' (OTP URLs); 'It is strongly recommended to only use password-protected backups.' Steam/Blizzard entries are excluded from the standard format.

findings.claim: Concrete designs to borrow for an AuthPeek 'Share' feature, each traceable to a source above.
findings.detail: (a) Two explicit tiers like Ente: 'Share codes' (no secret; pre-computed codes for 2/5/10 min; viewer shows current + next code, countdown bar, 'expired' and 'clock out of sync' states) vs 'Move account' (otpauth:// QR rendered on screen, never saved; optional otpauth-migration QR for Google Authenticator). (b) Ente-style link: random 256-bit key, AEAD ciphertext, key only after '#', static viewer page on GitHub Pages; go further than Ente by putting the ciphertext in the fragment too so nothing is transmitted (Excalidraw/PrivateBin pattern) and the same link can be pasted into the popup on another computer. (c) Expiry semantics from Bitwarden/1Password/Proton: short default (Ente 5 min for codes; 1Password 7 days default for items), explicit choice of duration, and honest UI that a serverless link cannot be revoked or view-limited (Keeper/Bitwarden need a server for device-lock and max access count). (d) Warnings taken from Google ('Never share your verification codes with anyone'), Proton (share over a secure channel; rotate/enable 2FA after), and Bitwarden (optionally send key separately). (e) Chrome Web Store hygiene: in-popup disclosure + consent on first use of Share, privacy-policy update naming GitHub Pages if ciphertext is ever transmitted, Limited Use statement on the site, Privacy practices tab updated for 'Authentication information'. (f) Fallbacks from Ente's desktop code and MDN compat: Copy link + QR first; navigator.share only when present and called from a click.

verifiedReviews.claim: A developer may not rate or review their own extension from any account, and reviews from affiliated people (which would include group-publisher members and friends acting on the developer's behalf) are treated the same way.
verifiedReviews.detail: Google's Spam policy FAQ (section "User ratings, reviews, and installs", last updated 2020-05-01) asks "Can I review or rate my own extension?" and answers: "No. Submitting a rating or review of your own extension, using your own account or other accounts, may be interpreted as an attempt to manipulate the extension's placement in the Chrome Web Store. This also includes ratings and reviews coming from other developers or users that are affiliated with the publisher." The same FAQ defines manipulating placement as "artificially manipulating how the Chrome Web Store orders and displays an extension" and says "Such practices are expressly forbidden." The consequence is in the Program Policies' "Best Practices and Guidelines" item 3: "No cheating. If you attempt to scam the system (for example, by misleading users, circumventing enforcement, copying the work of other developers, or manipulating your extension's reviews or ratings) you will be banned from the Chrome Web Store." The group-publishers doc (last updated 2026-04-15) says nothing about reviews. I found no Google documentation stating whether the store UI technically blocks the publisher account from submitting a rating (the user reports they "can't" do it); that mechanical detail is unconfirmed.

verdicts.reason: The claim is supported as stated by Google's own pages, and the cited quotes check out verbatim. (1) Spam policy FAQ (developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/spam-faq, "Last updated 2020-05-01 UTC"), Q "Can I review or rate my own extension?": "No. Submitting a rating or review of your own extension, using your own account or other accounts, may be interpreted as an attempt to manipulate the extension's placement in the Chrome Web Store. This also includes ratings and reviews coming from other developers or users that are affiliated with the publisher." Same page: "Manipulating placement refers to artificially manipulating how the Chrome Web Store orders and displays an extension. ... Such practices are expressly forbidden." (2) The FAQ is not orphaned: the current Program Policies page (developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/program-policies/policies, "Last updated 2025-05-22 UTC") links to it from the "Spam and Abuse" subsection ("For additional information about the spam policy, see the Spam FAQ"), and that subsection, item 2, says: "Developers must not attempt to manipulate the placement of any extensions in the Chrome Web Store. This includes, but is not limited to, inflating product ratings, reviews, or install counts by illegitimate means, such as fraudulent or incentivized downloads, reviews and ratings." The same page, "Best Practices and Guidelines" item 3: "No cheating. If you attempt to scam the system (for example, by misleading users, circumventing enforcement, copying the work of other developers, or manipulating your extension's reviews or ratings) you will be banned from the Chrome Web Store." The standalone Spam and Abuse policy page (developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/program-policies/spam-and-abuse, last updated 2022-11-01) carries the same item-2 text.
